title: Naming a service: how we chose a name for Share Homes for Ukraine data
authors: Denise Atkins, Content Designer, Homes for Ukraine Digital

content.content: A new start for Homes for Ukraine

The Homes for Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme was introduced in 2022 in response to Russia’s full scale illegal invasion of Ukraine. It enables Ukrainians fleeing the conflict to find safe accommodation with UK hosts.

You can read more about how our team created ‘Share Homes for Ukraine data’, our new, sustainable in-house system (or digital service) to support this humanitarian crisis, transitioning from emergency response to long-term transformation.
Moving on from the old platform

As the new system took shape, it was called by a variety of names. Some of these referenced the old platform, which we needed to move on from. At other times, it was referred to as ‘future tech’ or ‘the new thing’.
We didn’t want any of these internal nicknames to become embedded, as, from experience, they can be hard to shake off.
So, before we told users about the new system, we needed to decide on the name.
Bringing stakeholders with us
Deadlines were tight, so there wasn’t time for extensive user research around the name.

Naming can be an emotive topic, especially for the people closest to a service, so we needed to bring our stakeholders along with us. It was important that everyone understood the rationale behind the new name, particularly the people who would be guiding our users through the transition.
As the content designer on the team, I invited key stakeholders across the Homes for Ukraine digital and policy teams to a naming workshop.

I began by setting out the goals and expectations for the session. We didn’t want to go with the most popular choice. We weren’t going to vote for our favourites or make a final decision during the workshop.
Understanding good names
We established the naming architecture for the system, underneath the Homes for Ukraine service.
We looked at some good examples of existing service names:
We also looked at some confusing, "bad" names, that told us little about the product or service.
We agreed that a good name:
And the name will not:

I then took our stakeholders through the government Service Manual advice on naming a government service. The system isn’t public facing, so following the naming pattern for a government service wasn’t mandatory, although we still found the patterns a useful guide to ensure we created a name that would be accessible, trusted and understood.
After that, we got stuck into the mural board to put down all our ideas for describing the system. We used a series of prompts to inspire us:

We came up with over 50 words and phrases to describe the system. Between us, we organised these words into a quadrant. We ranked each word against two criteria. The vertical axis ranked words from ‘not task-focused’ at the bottom to ‘describes the task’ at the top. On the horizontal axis we ranked from ‘poetic’ to ‘plain English’.

That gave us a selection of words and phrases that sat in the top right corner, both describing the task and in plain English. We removed the other 3 sections and used a bigger version of the top right section to rank the best ones more ruthlessly, based on our acceptance criteria. We discussed these as a group and removed a few more that didn’t fit.
That gave us a selection of very strong contenders for the name.
Research and stress testing

Following the workshop, I discussed the shortlist in more detail with our Head of Product. We played around with a few alternatives, looking at words with similar meanings, and changing the order of the words. Others were removed as they weren’t suitable for certain potential use cases.
We agreed on the most suitable name, ‘Share Homes for Ukraine data’, plus a back-up using ‘Manage’ instead of ‘Share’.
Then I went off to conduct some final, desk-based research.
Existing service names
We didn’t want our name to clash with any other services or systems, so I explored what was already out there. I found nothing that overlapped with our name.

‘Data’ was a word that came up a lot in the workshop. It can sound like jargon, but it’s commonly used and much shorter than ‘information’. So, I checked to see if ‘data’ was used by other government services. I found a few that already had ‘data’ in the name, so we decided it was appropriate to use.
Checking user research

The user researchers on the Homes for Ukraine team did a quick review of their previous transcripts. That showed us the sort of words that came up naturally during our early discovery and user testing sessions with local authorities (LAs). This confirmed that our name used words the LAs were already familiar with. It reflected how they describe the tasks they perform on the system.
Avoiding bad names
I needed to check there weren’t going to be any embarrassing moments with the name, such as an initialism that spells something rude.

Also, while the system wasn’t going to be used by the public, it might still be talked about in front of the public. So, we wanted to check it didn’t sound silly or offensive in Ukrainian, as well as English.
Choosing and communicating the name

With all the due diligence complete, we agreed on Share Homes for Ukraine data. And because we didn’t want it abbreviated to an inaccessible acronym or an initialism, we decided on ‘Share’ as the official short, less formal version.

We told internal stakeholders the new name by email, explaining the process we went through and the rationale behind the final decision. We also explained how to capitalise the name, using sentence case for accessibility.
Our chosen name works because:
We also think Share sounds warm and humanitarian. This wasn’t among our acceptance criteria at the start, but it was a lovely bonus.
Stakeholder buy-in
The whole process was also fast, taking just a couple of weeks to prepare and run the workshop, synthesise the outputs, and decide on the name.
By taking stakeholders through the naming process with us, we ensured buy-in from key people. The final name was very well-received by all stakeholders.

With clear communication about the name, we avoided something different taking hold informally, before external communications had begun. We love the user-centred, task-focused name of our new system.

description: How do you choose a clear, accessible name for a new service? Find out how the Homes for Ukraine Digital team found a user-centred name that would work long term for its new system for managing Homes for Ukraine data.

title: Beyond the trees: how to make your woodland a wildlife haven

content.content: Healthy, species‑rich woodlands are more than a backdrop to rural life – they are working ecosystems that store carbon, slow water, protect soils and support livelihoods. The UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) treats biodiversity as an integral part of sustainable forest management across all woodland types, including ancient semi‑natural, native broadleaf, farm copses and productive conifers.

Diverse forests are better able to withstand pests, diseases and extreme weather events. They also provide the flexibility to meet your goals, whether that’s quality timber, nature recovery, public access or all three.
Understanding protected and priority species
Before you start woodland operations, it’s important to build up a picture of the wildlife on your site. Check local records and seek advice from your local Woodland Officer.

A woodland management plan that maps sensitive areas will help you to schedule work to avoid disturbing protected or priority species. For example, avoiding thinning near nesting sites in spring, retaining potential bat roost trees, or buffering watercourses that support species like Atlantic salmon or freshwater pearl mussel.
The aim is simple: stay legally compliant and take practical steps to help wildlife thrive while management work continues.
Special considerations for ancient woodland
Ancient woodlands, including ancient semi‑natural woodland (ASNW), wood pasture and parkland, and plantations on ancient woodland sites (PAWS), are irreplaceable.
For ASNW, keep trees native, avoid introducing invasive, non‑native species, protect veteran trees and soils, and manage deer and invasive shrubs.

For PAWS, plan progressive restoration and retain remnant ancient features. Thin and restructure your woodland to let light in, and favour natural regeneration of native species (where trees seed within the woodland habitat itself). Restoration strengthens resilience, supports specialist wildlife and leaves a legacy you can be proud of.
Getting the mix right

The UKFS embeds biodiversity into woodland design. Following best practice, manage at least 15% of your Forest Management Unit (FMU) with biodiversity as a major objective. Consider long‑term retentions such as riparian corridors (wooded areas alongside water bodies), native woodland blocks, open habitat networks, and deadwood hotspots.
Across your whole FMU, these simple ratios spread risk, create varied habitats and promote resilience without sacrificing productivity:
Deadwood as nature’s hidden infrastructure

Up to a fifth of woodland species depend on decaying wood.1 Plan to retain standing and fallen deadwood, especially large‑diameter native pieces in clusters around high‑value areas such as veteran trees, riparian zones, wood pasture and ancient woodland.

Over time, work towards roughly one lorry‑load per hectare (around 20 m³/ha). Manage safety hazards on well‑used trails, and where pests such as bark beetles are a concern, follow guidance on inspecting and removing specific host material after storms or periods of drought.
Connectivity and fragmentation

Wildlife moves through networks, so strengthening these connections within and beyond your boundary by linking habitats makes a real difference. Broaden rides and glades, build graded edges, retain hedgerows and veteran trees, and establish riparian corridors that stitch woods to the wider landscape.

When creating new woodland, extend from existing semi‑natural habitats to reduce edge effects. By expanding an existing habitat, you can maximise the safe interior ‘core’ of your woodland to limit the amount of vulnerable outer border exposed to harsh, external conditions. Design for connectivity but keep biosecurity in mind, by cleaning machinery and footwear, and control invasive non‑native species so that new links don’t become invasion routes.
Native woodland enhancement

Native woods carry the highest biodiversity value and are central to resilient landscapes. You can improve their ecological condition by controlling deer, grey squirrels and invasive shrubs, protecting soils, encouraging natural regeneration and having a diverse tree age and structure.

When creating new woods, choose site‑adapted native species and provenances (using certified reproductive material) and consider your site’s future climate. Converting appropriate non‑native stands near ancient woodland or along watercourses can deliver quick gains for wildlife and water quality.
Monitoring and assessment
Monitoring turns good intentions into results. It’s important to review your woodland management plan on a five‑year cycle. Keep it simple and carry out repeatable checks including:
The Woodland Wildlife Toolkit offers information and practical management guidance to better understand and care for your local woodland wildlife.
What this means for your objectives
Whether your aim is for habitat recovery, quality timber, natural flood management, farm diversification or public access – the UKFS gives you a single, practical framework to work from.

description: Neil Riddle, Head of Natural Environment at the Forestry Commission, explains how small, smart choices can turn your woodland into a wildlife hotspot while still producing timber and supporting long‑term resilience.

title: Slurry storage: sort it in summer, be winter-ready

content.content: In the middle of another hot, dry summer we can see our climate is changing. When we head into winter this translates into more rain, more runoff, and more pressure on slurry storage.  Getting ahead now can help protect your land, your business and the waterways your community depends on.

Slurry managed well is a resource. Slurry mismanaged is a pollution risk - to rivers, soils, and the communities downstream. The choices made now, in summer, shape what happens to those waterways come January.
At the Environment Agency we’re encouraging farmers to look at slurry storage requirements before the rain arrives. Now is the time to start planning for next winter.
With pressure on fuel and fertiliser prices, having plenty of spare capacity is not only vital for compliance, but also saves a valuable resource for when it’s most needed.
From an environmental point of view, spreading slurry during the winter months creates a significant pollution risk from run-off, damages soils and wastes valuable nutrients.
Spreading because your store is full, rather than because there is a soil or crop need, is also non-compliant with environmental regulations.
How much slurry storage capacity do I need?
The Silage, Slurry and Fuel Oil Regulations set out that all farms must have at least 4 months slurry storage.
If you’re in a Nitrate Vulnerable Zone, that requirement is higher.  Check what applies to your livestock type.
Farming Rules for Water also say you should not apply more than the soil and crop actually need, and you should not create a pollution risk.
We recommend a minimum of 6 months slurry storage to ensure meeting the requirements of Farming Rules for Water.
What can I do to prepare my slurry storage for winter?

Guttering that leaks or drainage that isn’t functioning properly can lead to an increase in slurry volume as clean rainwater mixes with manure in yards. Fixing any leaky pipes and gutters and making sure drains are free and running properly can make a difference. You may find these changes alone mean that your existing storage meets your requirements.
Use the AHDB slurry wizard to check how much slurry storage you need – this will show you if have enough storage to be compliant and to see you through the winter.
It can also help with planning for the future to assess the levels of capacity you may need for farm expansion, or to give you a buffer for contingency.
If your calculations show that you may not have enough storage, look at contingencies and get a plan in place to increase your storage capacity.
3. Plan for all eventualities
Whether you think you have enough storage capacity or not, making contingency plans could help you through if something unexpected happens.
Options to consider:

Read more about the guidance around storing slurry and planning a new store including notifying the Environment Agency at least 14 days before you build new storage for slurry or make substantial changes to an existing store.

Farmers can access Defra funding to improve slurry storage and management through the Capital Grant offer, expected to open 30 July. The Grant will fund items like automatic slurry scrapers, self-supporting covers for slurry and anaerobic digestate stores  and floating covers for slurry and anaerobic digestate stores and lagoons. Read the full guidance for Capital Grants here - Applicant's guide: Capital Grants 2026 - GOV.UK

Being ready for winter can help your business all year round. Only applying organic fertiliser during the growing season means that crops and grass take up more of the nutrients, increasing yields. Keeping machinery off wet soils not only protects the soil, but saves unnecessary fuel, wear and tear and man hours.
See how a Cornish dairy farmer tackles slurry storage challenges and transforms his farm to meet regulations.
Get in touch
If you have questions about preparing for winter, we can help – contact our national customer contact centre and ask to be put in contact with your local agriculture team.
Environment Agency National Customer Contact Centre
Email: enquiries@environment-agency.gov.uk
Other resources:
Farming Advice Service: https://www.farmingadviceservice.org.uk/technical-article/environment-agency-winter-ready-cab-card
Catchment Sensitive Farming: Catchment Sensitive Farming: advice for farmers and land managers - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk)

title: New date for Capital Grants 2026 webinar

content.content: The 2026 Capital Grants is expected to open on 30 July.
To help you prepare, we're hosting a webinar on 30 July for you to find out more. This webinar has been rescheduled from the original date of 22 July.
During the session you'll hear from me, and colleagues from the Rural Payments Agency (RPA). We will also cover the support provided by Catchment Sensitive Farming (CSF) (look at section 4.2).
We will explain which grant items may need CSF advice before you apply, and RPA colleagues will take you through the application and claims process.
We'll finish with a Q&A session, giving you the chance to ask questions and get answers from the team.
The webinar will start at 11am and finish at 12:30pm.
Register to attend.
If you can’t make it, don’t worry. We will publish a link to the recording once the webinar finishes.
For more information ahead of the webinar, do read my previous posts on Capital Grants and the Capital Grants 2026 guidance on GOV.UK.
This new round will make £225 million available which is 50% more than in 2025.
I look forward to seeing you there.

description: To help you prepare to apply for Capital Grants 2026, we're hosting a webinar on Thursday 30 July for you to find out more.

title: Learn more about the Farmer Welfare Grant

content.content: Earlier this month, we wrote a post introducing the Farmer Welfare Grant.
A total of £1.5 million will be available over 3 years to support farmer mental health and wellbeing across England.
The funding is intended to help rural and agricultural charities and organisations deliver practical support that strengthens both personal and business resilience across the sector.

While the application portal will not open until 6 August, we are sharing additional information in advance to help organisations considering an application. This includes details of 2 upcoming webinars.
Guidance, including the technical eligibility criteria, will be available when the portal opens.
Who can apply
Funding is only available to organisations with experience of supporting farming communities, not for individual farm businesses.
Any charitable or third-sector not-for-profit organisation registered in England can apply for funding if it can demonstrate its ability to deliver a suitable project.

For-profit organisations may also be eligible to apply as part of a consortium led by an eligible organisation, provided they can demonstrate how both the project and their role contribute to meeting the funding criteria.

We want grant recipients to develop support that responds to the specific needs of farming communities. For this reason, we are not prescribing the types of activities or approaches applicants should propose.
That said, applications that support the following priorities are particularly encouraged:

Funding can be used to cover both one-off and ongoing costs. This may include overheads, venue hire, materials, equipment, service delivery costs, and staffing costs where these are directly related to the project.
The exact number of projects will be determined by the amount and nature of applications we receive.
We’ll consider both individual projects and joint projects involving multiple organisations.
Applications are invited for grants of between £1,000 and £200,000 per year, covering expenditure incurred between November 2026 and March 2029.
How to apply
To apply, you must do so through an application portal. We will blog again when the portal opens.
As part of the application, you'll need to:
Once the application window has closed, the applications will be reviewed and scored by a team from Defra. Funding decisions will be made after all applications have been assessed.
Dates to note
Thursday 6 August – Application portal opens. Full guidance available.
Thursday 13 August, 2pm–3pm – Join our first webinar to learn more about the grant, guidance and eligibility criteria. A recording will be shared in this post after the session.
Monday 17 August, 10am–11am – Join our second webinar for a walkthrough of the application portal and application process. A recording will be shared in this post after the session
Wednesday 9 September, 11:59 am– Application portal closes.
Subscribe to the Farming Blog
For the latest updates on the Farmer Welfare Grant, subscribe to the Farming Blog.
By subscribing, you'll receive an email notification whenever we publish a new blog post.
